data.title: Amazon warns NYC delivery bill could add up to $5 per order
data.description:
Amazon said on Thursday legislation being considered by the New York City Council "could add up to $5" to each order, adding that it might be forced to consider moving operations outside the city if the bill passes.

  • Amazon said in a message to New York City customers that the council is weighing Intro 518, which it said could raise prices and affect how it delivers packages and groceries

  • The bill, sponsored by Councilmember Tiffany Caban, would require operators of last-mile delivery facilities to be licensed by the city and to directly employ delivery workers rather than contract the work out

  • Amazon said it works with a network of small delivery businesses and would no longer be able to work with them if the legislation passes

  • The company said moving operations outside the city would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers

  • Amazon said it is trying to work with the council and has invited every member to visit its delivery stations, and it has asked customers to contact their council member

data.description: Loblaw's pharmacy unit, Shoppers Drug Mart, shines in 3Q as prescription demand easily outpaced grocery growth. data.title: Cybersecurity Stocks Rally After Palo Alto Lifts Outlook, Inks AI Startup Deal
data.description:
By Connor Hart

Cybersecurity stocks rallied after Palo Alto Networks lifted its profit outlook and said it agreed to buy AI startup Applied Compute.

The cybersecurity company late Wednesday raised its outlook for the year, now expecting adjusted earnings of $4.26 to $4.30 a share. It also raised its outlook for next-generation security annual recurring revenue to be nearly $11.48 billion to $11.53 billion.

The higher outlooks came as Palo Alto agreed to buy Applied Compute, a San Francisco-based startup founded by former OpenAI researchers, in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion.

Applied Compute helps companies train and run custom AI models using proprietary data. It specializes in open-weight AI models, which allow users to download and modify the numerical values, called weights, that govern the models' behavior, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Shares of Palo Alto Networks jumped 9.6%, to $372.70, in premarket trading Thursday.

At the same time, a broader rally in cybersecurity stocks looks set to continue, with CrowdStrike, Cloudflare and Zscaler also rising premarket.

Shares of CrowdStrike rose 6.3%, to $252. Cloudflare's stock gained 5.6%, to $317.80, while Zscaler's popped 4.4%, to $206.50.

data.title: Scientists succeed in growing potatoes in simulated moon soil
data.description:
Key points:
  • Astronauts on moon bases will need locally grown food
  • NASA-backed study involved a potato variety called Modoc
  • Study used simulated lunar soil, plus organic material
  • Potatoes good source of starch, vitamins, minerals, fiber

By Will Dunham

Potatoes are one of the most important crops on Earth, a food that is a great source of starch, vitamins, minerals and fiber. They soon might be an important crop on the moon as well.

Scientists have now succeeded in growing nutritious potatoes in simulated lunar soil that are safe to eat, with an eye toward feeding astronauts who may staff bases on the lunar surface in the near future. They supplemented the lunar simulant with organic material, and found that with enough of it the potatoes grew just as well as they did in Earth soil.

The research, supported by NASA, involved a variety called Modoc, an early-maturing potato with red skin and white flesh.

The United States and China both intend to send astronauts to the lunar surface in the coming ⁠years, with plans for long-term bases on the moon. A local food source is considered vital ​for sustaining people staffing a moon base because of the impracticality of transporting all needed food from Earth.

"Potatoes provide more calories per land area than many other crops," said Oregon State University plant biologist Aymeric Goyer, who led the study published on Thursday in the journal npj Microgravity. "They are nutritious — they provide more potassium than a banana, are rich in vitamin C, have good proteins — and they have a high satiety index."

That means they are a very satisfying food, as fans of french fries already know.

The soil on the moon's surface is more properly called lunar regolith — basically crushed rock and dust, often sharp and glass-like, formed over billions of years by meteorite impacts. It lacks organic material, unlike Earth soil.

The researchers supplemented the simulated regolith with varying amounts of a nutrient-rich substance called vermicompost, produced when earthworms break down organic waste.

"Lunar regolith does not contain any nitrogen, so no crop would grow without supplementing it," Goyer said.

Potatoes planted in regolith with no vermicompost produced almost no roots or tubers.

The plants grew some roots and tubers with a mixture containing as little as 5% vermicompost and 95% regolith. With a mixture of 30% vermicompost, the yield was identical to potatoes grown under the same conditions in Earth soil — specifically from Hermiston, Oregon, a locale known for impressive potato yields.

The researchers grew the potatoes in a greenhouse under sunlight and artificial light, with the temperature at 72 degrees Fahrenheit (22 degrees Celsius) during the day and 64 F (18 C) at night.

So how did the potatoes taste?

"Unfortunately, we have not tasted them yet. We used what we harvested for lab analyses," Goyer said.

SMALL POTATOES

The plants in the current study were grown in small pots, so the potatoes they yielded were small, generally less than a third of an ounce (10 grams), even in Earth soil.

"We are working on a second study where we report on the growth of potatoes grown in larger pots. In this case, we obtained potatoes of size you typically see at the store," Goyer said.

Lunar regolith is hostile to crops also due to high levels of heavy metals like copper.

"Without organic matter, potatoes take up too much heavy metals, which can become toxic for the plants. Organic matter helps make heavy metals less available to the plants, so plants do not overaccumulate them," Goyer said.

Researchers have been experimenting with various crops for potential extraterrestrial agriculture. A study published in March documented chickpeas grown in lunar regolith supplemented with vermicompost.

"People are also working with tomatoes, lettuce and legumes like alfalfa," Goyer said.

While work on lunar agriculture is important for establishing a sustainable human presence on the moon, it also may offer benefits on Earth, according to Oregon State space biologist and study co-author David Handy.

"The technologies that are invented as a result can be used to produce food in regions of low agricultural output that are reliant on shipments, such as inner cities and desert communities. I believe continued research on the use of regolith will lead to techniques that can be used to improve soil quality, as well as remediate contaminated soils to improve sustainable agriculture here," Handy said.

Extraterrestrial potatoes already have germinated in popular culture, with a stranded astronaut played by actor Matt Damon harvesting them in a greenhouse on Mars in the 2015 film "The Martian." So could lunar fries, baked potatoes, aloo tikki and vichyssoise be on the menu at a future moon base?

"It is a very versatile crop, so yes, all the above. In terms of ease of preparation, maybe microwaved," Goyer said.

data.title: UBS seeks changes to final part of proposed Swiss banking overhaul
data.description:
UBS and the Swiss Bankers Association on Thursday called for significant changes to the last part of Switzerland's proposed banking stability reforms, arguing they went too far in response to the 2023 Credit Suisse collapse.

  • Their comments were a reaction to the conclusion of a public consultation on proposed new rules covering bank liquidity, resolution capacity and the powers of Swiss financial market regulator FINMA

  • The government proposals were made in response to the demise of Credit Suisse and its subsequent takeover by UBS

  • UBS, which has been at loggerheads with the government over new capital rules at the heart of the banking overhaul, said it rejects significant portions of the final package

  • "Substantial changes are needed to ensure that additional requirements are limited to demonstrated risks, aligned with international standards and are proportionate in their overall impact," UBS said

  • An assessment of the cumulative costs of all the so-called too-big-to-fail measures is still lacking, UBS said

  • The SBA backed steps to improve access to central bank liquidity in crises, but rejected broader powers for FINMA

  • The SBA also rejected the introduction of a senior managers regime as proposed by the government

  • Around 30 measures in the package could raise costs for banks, customers and the wider economy, SBA said

  • FINMA would get disproportionately far-reaching new powers under the plan, it added

data.title: Japanese Life Insurers Look Unlikely to Massively Shift From Foreign Markets — Market Talk
data.description: Japanese life insurance companies look unlikely to perform large-scale repatriation of investments from foreign markets into Japanese government bonds, J.P. Morgan analysts say in a note. At the moment, sales of foreign bonds to finance Japanese government bond purchases appear fairly limited, the analysts say. The insurers' current foreign assets are largely credit and stocks, which offer attractive returns and provide diversification benefits, they say. This makes a massive shift from foreign markets less likely, they say. Nonetheless, inflows into the Japanese market can't be ruled out. "A shift into JGBs cannot be ruled out if JGB yields rise substantially above yields on these [foreign] asset classes." (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

data.title: Stock Futures Rise Ahead of Anthropic Trading Debut — Update
data.description:
By Joe Stonor

Nasdaq futures led a rally in U.S. stocks premarket, after Anthropic's pricing of its hotly anticipated listing lifted confidence around the artificial-intelligence trade.

The expectation-beating IPO pricing of the company behind the Claude chatbot helped investor focus shift away from the AI jitters that have weighed on stocks so far this week. However, sentiment was tempered by hawkish Federal Reserve meeting minutes Wednesday that added to fears of extended policy tightening.

Nasdaq futures jumped 2% as chip makers and cloud-computing stocks rallied premarket. Anthropic sold more shares at a higher price than anticipated, implying a value of around $1.5 trillion for the company. S&P 500 futures were also in the green--up 1.2%--as the index looks to turn the tide on a fifth-straight day of losses. Contracts tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.6%. The index has fallen by more than 1% for three days in a row.

Equities were mixed across Asia, where the tech-dominated Nikkei Stock Average in Japan and South Korea's Kospi closed in the green. Stock indexes in Hong Kong and Shanghai fell, however. In Europe, major indexes were mixed as the continent-wide Stoxx 600 slipped 0.1%.

Treasury yields ticked higher after falling in Asian trade, as investors respond to a hawkish readout from the Fed's October meeting. Near-term rate-sensitive two-year yields rose above 4.800%, while 10-year yields nudged back toward 5.100%. Thirty-year yields hovered around 5.440%.

Oil prices rose, picking up from falls Wednesday after U.S. crude oil inventories rose for a second consecutive week. The benchmark Brent crude contract rose 1% to trade around $93 a barrel, while the West Texas Intermediate contract nudged up 0.9% to trade around $84 a barrel.

The dollar fell slightly, but remained close to its highest level against a basket of global currencies since January 2025. Copper prices steadied after falling sharply in the last session but gold extended losses, trading close to $3,700 a troy ounce. Bitcoin rallied after recent declines, adding over 2% to trade around $63,750.

Anthropic's trading debut will be in focus for the day ahead. Investors will also watch for readouts from the trilateral meeting between President Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen.

data.title: Saudi crude oil exports rise to seven-month high in September, data shows
data.description:
By Pablo Sinha

Saudi Arabian crude oil exports in September rose nearly 21% from August to 5.379 million barrels per day, the highest level since February, data from the Joint Organizations Data Initiative showed on Thursday.

Oil production rose about 34% to 8.37 million bpd from 6.24 million bpd in August.

Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter, and other members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries provide monthly export figures for publishing on the JODI website.

"Saudi crude exports had already started to recover in August, with a further rebound in September as the Kingdom utilised export terminals on both coasts," UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo said.

As exports increased, Saudi refinery crude throughput slipped 12,000 bpd to 2.285 million bpd in September from 2.297 million bpd the previous month, the data showed. Direct crude burning decreased by 143,297 bpd to 460,800 bpd.

Shipments from the Middle East have been severely disrupted since the US-Israeli war with Iran, which began at the end of February, led Iran to block exports through the Strait of Hormuz.

Fuel oil exports from Saudi Arabia are expected to maintain a robust pace, with Saudi Aramco issuing a fresh sales tender this week despite a refinery attack in late October, trade sources said.
